content.title: About
content.content: Canadian bacon is a lean cut of pork loin that is cured, smoked, and then cooked. Unlike traditional streaky bacon, it contains far less fat and has a tender, almost ham‑like texture. It is commonly used in breakfasts, salads, and classic North American dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name comes from its popularity in Canada, though it is now produced worldwide.
Traditional Canadian bacon is made from the pork loin, not the belly as with regular bacon.
Before cooking, the meat is usually smoked, giving it a distinctive flavor.
In the United States it is a key component of Eggs Benedict – poached eggs on an English muffin with bacon and hollandaise sauce.
Canadian bacon contains about 10 % fat, compared with roughly 30 % in regular bacon.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Provides roughly 12 g of protein per 100 g, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Source of vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 is essential for nervous system function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Contains zinc
items.content: Zinc supports immune function and wound healing.

items.title: Lower fat content
items.content: Compared with regular bacon, it has less saturated fat, making it a more moderate‑diet choice.

items.title: Provides iron
items.content: Iron is necessary for oxygen transport in the blood.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Curing and smoking add significant salt, which can be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Nitrites and nitrates
items.content: These preservatives used in smoking may be harmful in large amounts.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic or intolerant to pork products.

items.title: Cooking safety
items.content: Undercooked bacon may harbor pathogenic bacteria.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Canadian bacon can be pan‑fried, baked, or added to omelets, salads, sandwiches, and pasta dishes. It is often sliced thin and quickly browned to a golden crust. Serve hot or cold depending on the recipe.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the product in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at +4 °C for up to 5 days. For longer storage, freeze in a zip‑lock bag at –18 °C, where it remains good for up to 6 months. Before use, check for off‑odors or discoloration – signs of spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Cereal Rice Crispy Flavored are crunchy dry flakes made from whole grain rice, coated with a flavoring. They prepare quickly with just milk or yogurt and are suitable for breakfast or a snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain rice flakes retain most of the grain’s nutrients.
Flavorings can be natural (e.g., vanilla, strawberry) or artificial.
The product is often used in children’s meals because of its soft texture and mild taste.
Rice flakes are easily digestible and suitable for people with gluten intolerance.
The original recipe contains only rice, sugar, salt, and flavoring.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: The flakes contain a small amount of fat, making them suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Rice flakes provide quick‑release carbs that supply fast energy.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: When produced correctly, the product is free of gluten, important for those with celiac disease.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Their soft structure makes them easy on the stomach, beneficial for children and seniors.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Small amounts of B1 and B3 vitamins may be present, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Flavored flakes often contain added sugar, which can contribute to weight gain if consumed in excess.

items.title: Allergens
items.content: Flavorings may contain traces of nuts, dairy, or soy, which can trigger allergic reactions.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Rice flakes raise blood sugar quickly, a consideration for people with diabetes.

items.title: Possible additives
items.content: Some versions include artificial colors and preservatives that may not suit everyone.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour milk, kefir, yogurt, or a plant‑based drink over the flakes, add fruit, nuts, or honey. They are also used in desserts, bars, and as a crunchy topping for baked goods.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed package. For long‑term storage, keep in the refrigerator to prevent moisture absorption and loss of crispness.

rice-white-with-peas-fat-added.title: White Rice with Peas, Fat Added

content.title: About
content.content: White rice with peas, fat added is a ready‑to‑eat product consisting of boiled white rice mixed with cooked peas and a small amount of vegetable fat. It is commonly served in school cafeterias and as a quick meal for children and adults.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The rice‑pea combination provides a more complete amino‑acid profile than either ingredient alone.
This type of dish became popular in Soviet school meals during the 1970s.
Adding a modest amount of fat improves taste and aids absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.
White rice is quickly digested, while peas add fiber that moderates blood‑sugar spikes.
The product is often packaged in single‑serve pouches suitable for microwave heating.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Carbohydrates from rice combined with a bit of fat provide a fast and sustained energy supply.

items.title: Protein content
items.content: Peas contribute plant‑based protein essential for growth and tissue repair.

items.title: B‑vitamin complex
items.content: Both rice and peas contain thiamine, niacin, and folate, supporting metabolic processes.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Peas add fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Thermally processed ingredients make the product suitable for children and sensitive stomachs.

items.title: Fat content
items.content: Although modest, the added fat should be considered by those monitoring calorie intake.

items.title: Pea allergy
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to legumes, including peas.

items.title: High glycemic index of rice
items.content: White rice has a high GI, so people with diabetes should pair the product with protein or vegetables.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Heat the pouch in a microwave for 2‑3 minutes. It can be served as a standalone dish, added to vegetable stews, or used as a side with meat or fish.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place away from direct light. After opening, consume within 3‑5 days; discard if a rancid odor develops.

content.title: About
content.content: Corn taco shells are thin, crunchy tortillas made from whole‑grain corn flour, water and salt. They are a staple of Mexican cuisine, used for tacos, tostadas and many other dishes. The shell has a characteristic golden hue and a pleasant corn aroma.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Corn tortillas originated in Mexico over 3,000 years ago and form the basis of the traditional diet.
Traditionally they are cooked on a stone griddle (comal), but most are now mass‑produced in industrial ovens.
The corn used provides natural carotenoids, giving the shells their yellowish color.
Corn shells are gluten‑free, making them suitable for people with celiac disease.
In the United States more than 3 billion corn tortillas are consumed each year.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Corn shells contain dietary fiber that supports digestive health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with wheat tortillas, corn shells have a lower fat content, making them a lighter option.

items.title: Source of vitamin B6
items.content: Vitamin B6 is involved in protein metabolism and nervous system function.

items.title: Contains magnesium
items.content: Magnesium helps maintain normal muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Suitable for those avoiding gluten.

items.title: Corn allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to corn products.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Corn shells can raise blood sugar quickly, so people with diabetes should consume them in moderation.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some varieties contain added salt; choose low‑sodium options if you monitor sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use shells as a base for tacos, burritos, quesadillas, or as a crunchy side. Warm them on a skillet, microwave, or oven. For a softer texture, soak in hot water for a few minutes before filling.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep shells in an airtight package in a cool, dry place. For longer storage, refrigerate to prevent drying out. Discard any shells that develop mold or an off‑odor.
